analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for consumers to wipe out debts in bankruptcy by pushing more into repayment plans.
analysis.headline: The Senate first failed to cut off debate 53-45, then passed the companion bill 83-14 in February 2000, but the 106th Congress ended without it becoming law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite bankruptcy law to use a rigid income formula to decide who qualifies for a Chapter 7 discharge — a full wipeout of debts — and push everyone above the line into a Chapter 13 repayment plan. It would require credit counseling before filing, lengthen the waiting periods between bankruptcies, and make it harder to hold onto a home or car while paying down debts. It also includes genuine consumer protections: child support would jump to first priority, creditors who coerce debtors into reaffirming debts would face penalties, and retirement savings would be sheltered.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card issuers, banks, and other unsecured lenders, who would collect more from debtors who can no longer erase their bills. Family farmers get real relief through permanent Chapter 12 reenactment, custodial parents get first-priority treatment for support claims, and debtors gain new penalties against creditors who refuse reasonable repayment plans or bully them into reaffirming debts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card issuers and secured lenders

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a presumption of 'abuse' whenever a debtor's income exceeds a formula based on IRS expense standards, letting any party in interest move to dismiss or convert a Chapter 7 case into a Chapter 13 repayment plan, and rebutting the presumption requires detailed documentation of special circumstances.
Domestic support obligations — child support and alimony — move to first priority among claims, and discharge of debts is conditioned on certification that post-petition support payments were made.

The bill lets courts cut a creditor's claim by up to 20% if the creditor unreasonably refused a reasonable repayment plan proposed through approved credit counseling, makes threats to coerce debt reaffirmation a violation of the automatic stay, and directs the Attorney General to assign U.S. attorneys and FBI agents to abusive reaffirmation cases.
Individual debtors may exempt certain tax-exempt retirement funds from the bankruptcy estate.
The bill permanently reenacts Chapter 12 family-farmer bankruptcy relief and relaxes its eligibility test from one year to three years of majority farm income.

analysis.who_pays: Households in financial distress. The income formula decides who can get a fresh start using rigid IRS expense standards rather than actual living costs; debtors must complete credit counseling and a financial-management course before and after filing; debtors' attorneys face fee liability and civil penalties that make lawyers less willing to take marginal cases; the gap between Chapter 7 discharges stretches to eight years; and people with recent car loans and high home equity keep paying secured creditors instead of discharging those debts.

drawbacks.text: The means test presumes abuse whenever projected disposable income exceeds the lesser of $15,000 or 25% of unsecured claims over five years, and it can only be rebutted with itemized, documented special circumstances — a structure critics said would force many legitimately insolvent families into repayment plans based on formula expenses rather than real costs.

No individual could file for bankruptcy without first receiving a briefing from an approved nonprofit credit counseling service, and no discharge without completing a financial-management course — adding fees and delay for people at the point of financial collapse.

The bill extends the period between Chapter 7 discharges from six to eight years and between Chapter 13 discharges to five years, and requires debtors' attorneys to reimburse trustees and pay civil penalties if a court finds their Chapter 7 filing was not substantially justified, which raises the cost and risk of representation.

The bill erodes debtor protections in specific ways: liens on vehicles bought within five years of filing cannot be valued down, the automatic stay no longer blocks certain evictions, and the homestead exemption is cut back by a longer residency requirement.

Some provisions cut against lenders too — penalties for coercive reaffirmation practices and claim reductions for creditors who refuse reasonable repayment plans — so the industry bore limited costs alongside its gains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine mix of provisions, and an honest reading credits it: child support moves to the front of the line, retirement savings are sheltered, and creditors who bully debtors face real penalties. But the core of the bill — the income formula that decides who may erase debts — is a transfer of bargaining power from insolvent households to lenders. Because the formula uses standardized IRS expense allowances instead of what families actually pay for housing, transportation, and medical care, it would sweep in debtors who genuinely cannot repay. The counseling mandate adds cost without a demonstrated benefit. On balance, the main effect would be fewer full discharges and more money flowing to credit card issuers.

outcome.mechanism: After months of floor debate, the Senate passed the House companion, H.R. 833, in place of this bill by a 83-14 vote on February 2, 2000, and the record shows no further action before the 106th Congress ended, so it never became law.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on March 16, 1999 with nine original cosponsors from both parties, including Joseph Biden.
The Senate Judiciary Committee marked it up in April and reported it favorably with amendments on May 11, 1999, placing it on the calendar.
On September 21, 1999, cloture — the vote needed to end debate and move to a final vote — failed 53-45; all 53 votes to cut off debate came from Republicans and all 45 against came from Democrats.

The Senate returned to the bill from November 1999 through February 2000, and on February 2, 2000 it incorporated S. 625 into H.R. 833 and passed H.R. 833 in lieu of this measure by 83-14, with 50 of 55 Republicans and 33 of 45 Democrats in favor.
After that vote the measure was returned to the calendar, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 without the bill becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, financially distressed households kept the existing bankruptcy system's broader access to a full Chapter 7 discharge, and lenders did not collect the additional repayment-plan revenue the means test would have produced. The consumer protections the bill contained also never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financially struggling debtors kept current law

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1999 and shepherded it through Senate floor debate.

for.name: Orrin Hatch and the Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held markups in April 1999 and reported the bill favorably with amendments on May 11, 1999.

for.name: 53 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Provided every vote to invoke cloture on September 21, 1999, and later supplied 50 of the 83 votes passing the companion bill.

for.name: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
for.what_they_did: Spent years lobbying for a means test to shift more debtors into repayment plans, making this one of the era's most heavily lobbied bills.

against.name: 45 of 45 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Every Democratic senator voted against cutting off debate on September 21, 1999, blocking the bill from a final vote at that stage.

against.name: 14 senators who voted no on final passage
against.what_they_did: Voted against passing the companion bill H.R. 833 on February 2, 2000.

against.name: Edward Kennedy
against.what_they_did: Led floor opposition and used holds and debate to slow the bill, tying it to demands to raise the minimum wage.

against.name: Consumer groups, unions, and bankruptcy professionals
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the means test as too rigid for families facing job loss, illness, and divorce.

sides.party_line_note: The first test split perfectly by party — all 53 cloture votes came from Republicans, all 45 votes against from Democrats — but the final 83-14 passage in February 2000 drew support from 33 of 45 Democrats, with 12 Democrats and 2 Republicans still opposed.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and unsecured consumer lenders
industries.note: The means test would move debtors who can technically repay a fraction of their debts out of Chapter 7 liquidation and into multi-year Chapter 13 repayment plans, so lenders collect more of what they are owed instead of writing it off. The industry gains come directly at the cost of insolvent households' fresh start, though the bill also imposes penalties on lenders who refuse reasonable repayment plans or coerce debt reaffirmation.

The bill bars anyone from filing for bankruptcy without a briefing from an approved nonprofit credit counseling service and conditions discharge on completing a financial-management course, making these agencies a mandatory gateway for every debtor. That guarantees them a captive client base even as the quality and value of the counseling remain unproven.

industries.industry: Secured lenders — auto lenders and mortgage holders
industries.note: The bill lets secured creditors keep their liens through Chapter 13, ends the ability to value down vehicles bought within five years of filing, and shortens the windows in which debtors can retain collateral without acting. Household debtors keep paying these creditors rather than discharging the debt.

Title IX exempts swap and netting agreements from the automatic stay and shields asset-backed securitization transfers from the bankruptcy estate, letting financial contract counterparties exit positions immediately and keep collateral out of the pool available to other creditors.

The bill permanently reenacts Chapter 12 family-farmer bankruptcy relief and relaxes the eligibility test from one year to three years of majority farm income, giving struggling farmers a reorganization path they would otherwise lose.
